author.name: JJ Marr
author.headline: Scaling Production LLM Orchestration | SDE 2 @ AMD, B. Eng

replies.text: Horace Chan Easier said than done when my AIs can spawn thousands of gcc processes each to debug a template issue. Gimme access and I'll DDoS you in a week.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
JJ Marr there is why you need your personal MI300 server.   192 cores. 8 GPU, 1TB of RAM all to yourself.  It will take lots of processes to crash it.   

And I wrap the sub agent run with slurm, which is a job dispatcher for HPC, probably way over engineered for what I do.  But since the infrastructure is there, might as well use it.

author.name: JJ Marr
author.headline: Scaling Production LLM Orchestration | SDE 2 @ AMD, B. Eng

replies.text:
Horace Chan if only I could afford that! But I don't want to spend my own money on build systems even though for C++, I can get parallelism in the thousands of jobs for a suitably sized codebase.

I wouldn't call slurm overengineered. It's underengineered compared to other options for distributed builds. 

We could adopt something like Bazel or Buck2 & provide a company wide Remote Build Execution service. A distributed hermetic build system with caching of artifacts would save me hours every week.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: JJ Marr there is a few perks of being a PMTS.  I can get access to those servers even though it is kind of a waste of resources to use it on my tasks straightly speaking.  But it is cool to push the limit without worrying, so why not.  I am so spoiled that I get the habit of using RAM disk for most of my work.  If you want speed, nothing beats RAM disk.
